rejected.title: Fines
card: A fine is a sanction where the offender pays a sum of money to the state. It is the least serious of the main sanctions, and it does not remove the offender's freedom.
The court sets the amount by looking at the offence. A more serious offence usually brings a larger fine, up to the limit the law allows for that offence.
The court also looks at the offender's ability to pay. The same fine can hurt a person on a low income much more than a person on a high income.
A fine can punish the offender, deter them from reoffending and deter others from offending. It is often used for less serious offences, such as minor traffic matters.
rejected.remember: A fine is money paid to the state, set by how serious the offence is and what the offender can afford.

a.q: Which statement best describes a fine?
opts: Money paid to the state by the offender
Money paid to the victim by the offender
Unpaid work done in the community
Time spent under supervision by a court officer
a.why: A fine is a sum of money paid to the state, not to the victim. Unpaid work and supervision are conditions of a community correction order, which is a different sanction.
a.clue: Think about who receives the money.

b.q: Two drivers in Geelong are found guilty in court of the same minor speeding offence. Sam earns a very high income. Jo is a student with little money. How does the court approach setting their fines?
opts: It considers what each driver is able to pay
It sets one amount, whatever each driver can pay
It gives Jo a larger fine, as she has less money
It looks at their incomes but not at the offence
b.why: The amount is set by the offence and also by the offender's ability to pay, so the court considers each driver's means. Setting one amount whatever each can pay is tempting because the offence is the same, but it ignores ability to pay.
b.clue: Two things help set the amount: the offence and what the offender can afford.

b.q: Two drivers in Geelong are found guilty of the same minor speeding offence. Sam earns a very high income. Jo is a student with little money. Which approach to their fines fits the card?
opts: The court may weigh what each person can afford to pay
The court must set the same amount, whatever each can pay
The court must set a larger fine for Jo, who has less money
The court looks only at the driver's past, not the offence
b.why: The amount is set by the offence and also by the offender's ability to pay, so the court can take each driver's means into account. Setting the same sum whatever the means ignores ability to pay, which is the tempting wrong answer.
b.clue: Two things help set the amount: the offence and what the offender can afford.

a.best: Money paid to the state by the offender

b.best: The court may weigh what each person can afford to pay

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a soft 'may'. Every distractor uses an absolute: 'must' (twice) or 'only'. A test-wise student can pick the hedged option without knowing the idea.

'deter them and others from reoffending' is slightly inaccurate. General deterrence stops others from offending at all, not from reoffending. It should read 'deter them from reoffending and others from offending'.
